Complete Empirical Research Plan  

──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────  

1. Identification Strategy  
Strategy: Continuous-treatment difference-in-differences (TWFE panel fixed-effects).  

Why appropriate  
• Weather realizations (temperature and precipitation anomalies) are plausibly exogenous, varying across countries (c) and over years (t).  
• Panel fixed effects purge time-invariant country characteristics (soil quality, institutions) and global shocks (commodity prices, financial crises).  
• “Differences” come from within-country deviations from the long-run mean (“weather shocks”) relative to other countries in the same year → a DiD design with a continuous, re-occurring treatment.  
• Allows dynamic effects by adding leads/lags (event-study style).  
• Simpler and more transparent than IV or RDD for this question; no adoption timing issues.  

2. Treatment and Control  
Treatment variable  
Tct = standardized anomaly of average growing-season temperature (°C) in country c, year t.  
Pct = standardized anomaly of growing-season precipitation (mm).  
Either variable can be entered linearly and in quadratic form, or discretized into “hot/dry shock” dummies (e.g., |anomaly| > 1 σ).  

Control group / counterfactual  
Observations in the same year that experience smaller (or opposite-signed) anomalies. The counterfactual for a “hot year” in country c is that same country in years without a hot shock, plus other countries in year t.  

Treatment timing  
Year t when the anomaly occurs (repeated, not once-and-for-all). If an event-study is run, t = 0 is the shock year; leads t = −3…−1 test pre-trends, lags t = 1…3 capture persistence.  

No running variable / cutoff (not an RDD).  

3. Key Identifying Assumptions  
A1. Parallel trends: In the absence of a weather shock, treated and untreated observations would have followed the same trend in outcomes. Plausible because we difference out country and year FEs and because short-term weather is random. Testable via event-study pre-trends.  

A2. Exogeneity of weather: Conditional on fixed effects, weather anomalies are as-good-as-random. Supported by meteorological evidence; economic agents cannot manipulate annual average temperature or rainfall.  

A3. SUTVA / no cross-country spillovers: A shock in country c does not immediately alter weather in country d. Reasonable, although commodity-price spillovers could transmit economic effects; we address this by controlling for world crop prices.  

A4. Stable composition: No systematic entry/exit of countries in sample correlated with shocks. Check by confirming balanced panel or adding inverse-probability weights.  

4. Main Threats and Mitigation  
T1. Global commodity-price channel: A drought in large exporters could raise world prices and benefit other countries, violating SUTVA. Mitigation: control for world cereal price index; cluster SEs two-ways (country and year) to allow arbitrary correlation.  

T2. Serial correlation & long memory in weather: Could under-state SEs. Mitigation: cluster by country, apply Newey–West with 3-lag bandwidth, and run randomization inference (permutation of shocks within countries).  

T3. Adaptation / different trend slopes: Hotter countries may adapt over time (heterogeneous trends). Mitigation: interact country-level long-run climate normals with year fixed effects, or use country-specific linear trends. Also estimate heterogeneous effects by baseline climate quintiles.  

5. R Code Outline  

```r
# 0. Packages
library(data.table)  # fast data handling
library(fixest)      # TWFE & event-study
library(lmtest); library(sandwich)

# 1. Load data -----------------------------------------------------------
d <- fread("weather_econ_panel.csv")   # country, year, temp, precip, ag_output, gdp_growth

# 2. Construct variables -------------------------------------------------
# Long-run country-specific means (1980-2010 baseline for example)
baseline <- d[year %between% c(1980, 2010),
              .(temp_mu = mean(temp, na.rm=TRUE),
                precip_mu = mean(precip, na.rm=TRUE)), by = country]

d <- merge(d, baseline, by="country")

# Weather anomalies (standardized by country σ)
d[, `:=`(temp_sd   = sd(temp,   na.rm=TRUE),
         precip_sd = sd(precip, na.rm=TRUE)), by = country]

d[, temp_anom   := (temp   - temp_mu)   / temp_sd]
d[, precip_anom := (precip - precip_mu) / precip_sd]

# Discrete shock indicator
d[, hot_shock  := (temp_anom   > 1)]
d[, dry_shock  := (precip_anom < -1)]

# 3. Main specification --------------------------------------------------
# Outcome 1: log agricultural output
est1 <- feols(log(ag_output) ~ temp_anom + I(temp_anom^2) + precip_anom +
              I(precip_anom^2) | country + year,
              data = d, cluster = ~country)

# Outcome 2: GDP growth
est2 <- feols(gdp_growth ~ temp_anom + precip_anom | country + year,
              data = d, cluster = ~country)

etable(est1, est2, se.below = TRUE)

# 4. Event-study (dynamic DiD) ------------------------------------------
# Create event time for hot shocks
setorder(d, country, year)
d[, hot_event := shift(hot_shock, type="lag")!=1 & hot_shock==1, by = country]
d[, event_time := sequence(.N) - which(hot_event==TRUE)[1], by = country]
# Keep only window −3..+3
d_es <- d[event_time %between% c(-3,3)]

ev <- feols(log(ag_output) ~ sunab(event_time, hot_event) | country + year,
            data = d_es, cluster = ~country)
iplot(ev)

# 5. Robustness: country-specific linear trends --------------------------
est_trend <- feols(log(ag_output) ~ temp_anom + precip_anom |
                   country + year + country[year],
                   data = d, cluster = ~country)

etable(est1, est_trend)
```

6. Expected Results  
Theory (heat-stress and water-stress in crop physiology) predicts:  
• One-standard-deviation hotter growing season → ≈ 2–4 % fall in agricultural output.  
• Pass-through to GDP growth smaller, roughly −0.3 to −0.7 pp, larger in ag-intensive economies.  

7. Validity Checklist Self-Assessment (DiD)  
C1: Parallel pre-trends verified with event-study. → 1  
C2: Exogeneity / no manipulation of treatment. → 1  
C3: No anticipation (farmers cannot foresee anomalies one year ahead perfectly). → 0.8  
C4: No interference / spillovers across units. → 0.5 (commodity channel).  
C5: Correct standard-error inference for serial correlation. → 1 (clustered + NW).  

Total ≈ 4.3 / 5.
